answers.answer: The caller supplies a known key to retrieve its associated value. Use an unambiguous tuple encoding of tenant ID, device ID, and record kind settings; encode or escape each part consistently so separators inside IDs cannot collide. Store the complete settings record as the value because the lookup reads those settings together. Including tenant prevents repeated device IDs from colliding, and record kind distinguishes settings from status. This is authoritative source-of-truth data, not necessarily a disposable cache copy. Key-value access alone makes no crash-survival promise; verify persistence and failure guarantees. Replacement puts first store {mode: quiet, color: green}, then leave only {mode: loud}; get returns {mode: loud}. Delete removes it, and a get observing deletion reports absence. A timeout only means no result arrived, so existence is unknown and must not be treated as confirmed absence. The key identifies data but does not authorize its use; verify the caller has access to that tenant and record.

evidence.quote: The key-value label says nothing by itself about whether acknowledged writes survive a crash.
The old color field is gone.
A get timeout means no result arrived. It does not tell you whether the key exists.
Use an unambiguous encoding of those parts.
A key selects data; it does not grant permission.

answers.answer: A known equipment ID identifies a single record, but region = west supplies a field value rather than the matching IDs. Merely placing region in each value creates no efficient region lookup. A scan inspects entries and filters values; work grows with entries inspected even when few match, and filtering cannot undo those reads. An index maps west to candidate equipment IDs, then fetches the needed records without examining every value. It consumes storage and update work: moving a record between regions or deleting it must update the index. Verify who maintains it and when it reflects writes; an application-maintained index requires coordination. Basic key-value access does not promise secondary indexes, so verify actual support.

evidence.quote: Storing the city inside each value does not create an efficient lookup by city.
Filtering the results does not undo the reads already performed.
When a record moves cities or is deleted, the index must change too.
Some stores supply indexes or ordered range queries; basic key-value access promises neither.

answers.answer: Both blind writes store 21, so the final count is 21 instead of the intended 22: one increment is lost although both writes may succeed. With atomic version checks, each worker attempts a put conditional on version 7. The first successful attempt writes 21 and advances the version, for example to 8. The other attempt finds the version no longer 7 and is rejected without applying its stale write. That worker rereads 21 and the current version, recomputes 22, and conditionally writes against that version, advancing it on success. Bound retries if contention continues. A separate check followed by an unconditional put leaves a gap where another worker can change the record; the condition and update must be indivisible. This protects the one key, not automatically several keys or an external action.

evidence.quote: Tests a condition and changes the value as one indivisible operation.
Only one update based on the old version succeeds.
The rejected caller rereads the current value and version, recomputes its change and makes another conditional attempt.
Checking the version in a separate request before an unconditional put leaves the same race.

answers.answer: The request may have completed while its reply was lost, so timeout leaves execution unknown. Repeating an identical replacement with no intervening write leaves the same value. Retrying an add-one operation can add twice, even when each execution is atomic. Duplicate prevention needs the same operation ID and intent on every retry, recognition of duplicates, and atomic coordination of recording the ID with changing the data; retain duplicate records throughout the retry window and verify product support and scope. Without verified protection, reconcile the uncertain increment through application recovery instead of blindly retrying; use bounded retry/backoff for retryable failures. An unconditional replacement retry can also overwrite an intervening newer value. TTL triggers expiration by an entry lifetime rule; eviction removes entries for capacity pressure under configured policy. Eviction can precede TTL, so TTL does not promise retention until the deadline. Neither mechanism refreshes removed data; a cache may reload from its source, while authoritative data requires retention and recovery planning. Expiration is not an exact-time business scheduler: enforce access deadlines during authorization and use a suitable work-execution mechanism for timed actions. Verify TTL support, expired-data visibility versus physical deletion timing, eviction settings, and documented retry/condition/operation-identity guarantees. The lesson does not specify a particular recovery implementation or timed-work product.

evidence.quote: A write can finish and its reply can be lost.
Executing an increment twice adds twice, even if each increment is individually atomic.
A request ID alone is insufficient: recording it and changing the data must be coordinated atomically, with duplicate records retained for the retry window.
An entry can disappear before its TTL; a TTL is not a promise to retain it until the deadline.
Neither removal mechanism fetches a fresh replacement.
Expiration is also not a scheduler promising that business work runs at the exact deadline.
Check TTL support, expiry visibility and eviction configuration in the chosen implementation before relying on any of them.

answers.answer: A partition is a portion of the keyspace assigned to a storage node or group. Spreading key groups can spread storage and request work for workloads using many keys. If most requests hit one hot key, adding partitions may leave its serving capacity as the bottleneck; measure actual request distribution rather than just key count. A lagging replica is a maintained copy that may not yet expose the successful write, and a read mode permitting stale results can return the older value. This is a read-consistency issue: which writes a read is guaranteed to observe. Durability instead concerns whether acknowledged data survives specified failures. Durable data may still be missing from a stale read, and observing new data does not prove crash survival. Verify implementation guarantees, persistence and replication settings, and selected read/write modes before promising latest reads or survival of acknowledged writes; node count and acknowledgement alone establish neither.

evidence.quote: A portion of the keyspace assigned to a storage node or group.
More partitions alone may not help when most work still targets that key's serving capacity.
A durable write can still be absent from a lagging read.
Check the implementation, persistence and replication settings, and the selected read/write mode.

answers.answer: A is a direct fit: the known key retrieves the complete independent preferences record without a discovery scan, and replacement matches its access pattern. B needs more than basic lookup: changing filters can force scans that read extra data or indexes and duplicated records that add update work; application-side joins add requests and coordination. A richer query or transaction-capable store may fit B better, and a product may support several access models. For A, verify authorization of the account record so knowing or guessing a key cannot expose another account's preferences. Also verify durability under the required failures and persistence settings if these preferences are the authoritative copy, because an acknowledged update must survive the failures the service promises to tolerate. The access model alone proves neither speed nor safety: network, value size, hot keys and implementation limits affect performance, and correctness depends on the required guarantees and configuration. Measure representative requests and failures.

evidence.quote: Independent records fetched and replaced by a known key are a direct fit.
Scans read extra data; indexes and duplicated records add update work; application-side joins add requests and coordination.
A guessed key must not bypass that check.
Check the store's persistence settings and failure guarantees before using it as the only copy.
A known-key lookup can avoid unnecessary search, but network, value size, hot keys and implementation limits still affect latency and capacity.
